# On the Peculiar Beauty of Ordinary Moments

I've been thinking lately about how we photograph sunsets but rarely photograph the moment just before, when the light is still ordinary, the sky still blue, and nobody's phone is out yet. There's something almost defiant about those pre-golden-hour moments—they exist in perfect indifference to their own ordinariness, unaware that in twenty minutes they'll be gone, replaced by something we'll all collectively decide is worth documenting.

This might be the central tragedy of human consciousness: we're built to notice the exceptional, which means we're almost architecturally incapable of appreciating the everyday until it's safely behind us. I think about my grandmother's kitchen—the harvest gold appliances, the linoleum with the pattern worn smooth in front of the sink, the way afternoon light came through the window and made everything look like an old photograph even when it was happening in real time. I have almost no memories of being conscious that I was happy there, yet I would trade small things to smell it again.

We're always preparing for the next moment, optimizing for it, planning around it. Last week I caught myself mentally reviewing a conversation while still in the middle of having it. The other person was talking, and I was already several sentences ahead, checking their words against my internal script of how I thought they'd perform. It's like we're all method actors who forgot we're actually supposed to be present for the scene.

There's a genre of self-help literature built on the premise that if we could just be more present, more mindful, more conscious of the moment we're in, we'd be happier. And maybe that's true, but I suspect it's also fundamentally difficult in a way that no amount of meditation cushions can fix. Our brains developed to keep us alive, not to feel peaceful. The wandering mind that checks for threats in the peripheral vision, the attention that shifts toward novelty and change—these are features, not bugs, even if they make it hard to simply sit with a cup of tea.

But here's what I find interesting: sometimes it sneaks up on you anyway. Sometimes you're doing something completely mundane—waiting in a checkout line, driving home, sitting in a waiting room reading a magazine from 2019—and you suddenly become aware that you're alive, that this is your life, that this moment is real. And it's neither good nor bad; it's just the texture of existing. Those moments are rare enough that I've started paying attention when they happen, like I'm collecting data on when consciousness decides to announce itself.

I think maybe the secret is that you can't actually make yourself present the way the self-help books suggest. It's too willful, too tense. It's like trying to fall asleep by concentrating really hard on falling asleep. Instead, presence seems to arrive in the margins—when you're distracted enough to stop trying, when you've given up on optimizing, when you've simply accepted that nothing particular is happening and that's actually fine.

A lot of life is waiting, when you think about it. We're waiting for the next phase, the next achievement, the next version of ourselves that will finally be satisfied. We're always in the waiting room, checking our phones, wondering how much longer. And meanwhile, the waiting is the life. The waiting room is the room we're in.

I've also been thinking about how we use language to collapse time. We say "I'm stressed about the future" as if the future is here now, as if we're currently living in something that hasn't happened yet. And maybe we are, in a sense—we're living in our mental model of the future, not in the present. The actual future, when it arrives, will almost certainly be different from what we imagined. But we'll have spent real time, real conscious moments, living in the wrong mental space.

This might sound like I'm advocating for pure carelessness, for never planning or thinking ahead. I'm not. We have to think ahead; that's part of being human. But there's a difference between planning and colonizing the present with anxiety about the future. There's a difference between remembering the past and being haunted by it.

What I keep coming back to is how much beauty is absolutely free and available, and how we walk past it constantly because we're too busy or too tired or too worried. Not the sunset-beauty that requires being in the right place at the right time. I mean the free beauty: the way light falls through leaves, the way people's faces change when they laugh, the fact that we can taste things, that music exists, that language lets us share thoughts that exist only in our individual minds.

When I was very young, I could look at a rock for what felt like a long time, genuinely interested in it. I could watch an ant work and feel like I was learning something profound. Somewhere along the way, that capacity didn't disappear, but it got buried under efficiency and purpose and the constant low hum of things to do.

I don't have a conclusion to this. I don't think there's a solution, some trick you can learn that will make you permanently present and happy. I think it's something you have to practice the way you practice any skill—by doing it imperfectly, over and over, forgiving yourself when you zone out and end up three thoughts ahead again.

But I do think it's worth noticing, worth trying, worth caring about. Because the time you're in right now—boring, ordinary, just a random Tuesday—is the only one you actually get to live. The exceptional moments are going to take care of themselves. It's the unremarkable ones that need a witness.

And maybe that witness can be you.
